scenario: Your API calls a recommendation service with no timeout. When that service hangs, all of your API's worker threads end up stuck waiting and the whole site stops responding.
prompt: What is the first thing to add?

options.text: A bigger server for the recommendation service
A timeout on the call, with a fallback when it fires

explanation: Without a timeout, one slow dependency holds every thread hostage. A short timeout plus a fallback (for example, no recommendations) keeps the core site up. More threads just take longer to all get stuck.

scenario: Each user may make 5 requests per second on average, but short bursts of up to 20 requests should be allowed.
prompt: Which rate limiting algorithm fits?

options.text: Token bucket: refill 5 tokens/s, bucket size 20
Fixed window: at most 5 requests per calendar second
Block the user after 20 total requests
An unbounded queue for every user

explanation: A token bucket enforces the average rate through its refill speed and allows bursts up to the bucket size. A 5-per-second fixed window would reject any burst.

scenario: During a network partition between two data centers, the shopping cart service keeps accepting writes in both.
prompt: What did it give up, and what must it handle later?

options.text: Availability; it must replay the rejected writes
Strong consistency; it must merge conflicting carts when the partition heals
Durability; it must restore from backups

explanation: Staying available on both sides of a partition means the two copies can diverge (an AP choice under CAP). When the link returns, the carts must be reconciled, for example by merging their items.

prompt: Why run at least two instances of a service in different availability zones?

options.text: If one zone goes down, the other keeps serving traffic
It is cheaper than one instance

explanation: Availability zones fail independently (power, network). Spreading instances across them removes a single point of failure.

scenario: A downstream service is failing. Your code keeps calling it on every request, each call waits for a timeout, and your own latency balloons.
prompt: Which pattern helps?

options.text: Retry each failed call five times immediately
A circuit breaker that fails fast for a while, then tests whether the service recovered

explanation: After enough failures the breaker opens and calls fail instantly instead of waiting. After a cool-down it lets a few test calls through and closes again once they succeed.

scenario: Last month the whole site was down for 40 minutes when a single virtual machine rebooted.
prompt: Tap the single point of failure.
explanation: Everything else is redundant, but every request needs the auth service and it runs on one instance with no failover. When its VM rebooted, nothing could authenticate.

prompt: Put the steps of handling a production incident in order.

options.text: An alert fires on the rising error rate
Mitigate: roll back or fail over to restore service
Investigate and confirm the root cause
Write a blameless postmortem with action items

explanation: Restore service first, then dig into the root cause once users are no longer affected, then capture lessons so it does not recur.

scenario: The recommendation service is down. The product page normally shows a 'You might also like' row from it.
prompt: What should the product page do?

options.text: Retry until the recommendation service answers
Show the page without that row, or with a cached default list

explanation: Graceful degradation: a non-essential feature failing should not take down the core experience. Customers can still view and buy the product.

scenario: After you post, you see your own post immediately, but your friends only see it a few seconds later.
prompt: Which consistency model describes this system?
explanation: Everyone converges on the same data after a delay (eventual), and the author is guaranteed to see their own write right away (read-your-writes). Strong consistency would show friends the post immediately too.

scenario: Each API instance's health check endpoint runs a database query. During a 20-second database blip, the load balancer marks every API instance unhealthy and removes all of them.
prompt: What is the best fix?

options.text: Health-check every 1 second instead of every 10
Keep the load balancer check shallow (is this process alive?), and alert on dependency health separately

explanation: A shared dependency in the health check makes every instance fail at once, turning a brief database blip into a total outage. The load balancer should only remove instances that are themselves broken.

prompt: Which item is an SLI rather than the target SLO?

options.text: The measured fraction of successful requests

explanation: An SLI is a measured service characteristic. An SLO specifies the target for that indicator over a defined scope and window. Source: [Google SRE objectives](https://sre.google/sre-book/service-level-objectives/)

prompt: What failure count corresponds to the entire error budget?
scenario: The window contains exactly 1,000,000 eligible requests. The SLO is 99.9% successful requests, with every request weighted equally.
explanation: For this request-based objective, 0.1% of 1,000,000 is 1,000 failed requests. This is not a time-based downtime calculation. Source: [Google SRE objectives](https://sre.google/sre-book/service-level-objectives/)

prompt: Which latency view exposes the users hidden by the average?
scenario: Most requests remain fast, but around 2% now take several seconds. The team wants to see that slow tail.

options.text: High latency percentiles such as p99

explanation: Tail latency shows the slow fraction of requests that an average can hide. Inspect successful and failed requests separately as well. Source: [Google SRE monitoring](https://sre.google/sre-book/monitoring-distributed-systems/)

prompt: What is the maximum number of database calls for one API request?
scenario: An API can call a worker three times. Each worker attempt can call a gateway three times; each gateway attempt can call the database three times. All attempts fail.
explanation: If all three layers independently make up to three attempts and every attempt reaches the next layer, the leaf can see 3 × 3 × 3 = 27 attempts. Retries can multiply load. Source: [AWS Builders Library](https://aws.amazon.com/builders-library/timeouts-retries-and-backoff-with-jitter/)

prompt: What reduces synchronization when many clients retry at the same backoff times?
scenario: Clients use identical exponential backoff intervals after an outage. Their retries form recurring traffic spikes.

options.text: Make all clients use one fixed retry timestamp
Add jitter to the bounded backoff policy

explanation: Jitter randomizes retry timing so clients do not all return together. Keep retries bounded and budgeted; random delays alone do not fix an overloaded dependency. Source: [AWS Builders Library](https://aws.amazon.com/builders-library/timeouts-retries-and-backoff-with-jitter/)

prompt: Tap the queue whose unbounded backlog defeats the request deadlines.
scenario: Requests have a one-second end-to-end deadline, but the server’s waiting queue already takes ten seconds to drain. Workers keep starting expired requests.
explanation: Bounding queues and shedding overload can avoid spending scarce capacity on requests that cannot meet their deadlines. More queued work is not automatically useful work. Source: [Google SRE overload](https://sre.google/sre-book/handling-overload/)

prompt: Tap the resource pool that should be isolated from optional work.
scenario: Slow recommendation calls consume every connection in a shared pool. Checkout is healthy but cannot get a connection.
explanation: Bulkheads partition resources so one failing part cannot consume all capacity needed by another. Separate bounded pools make that isolation explicit. Source: [Azure Bulkhead](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/patterns/bulkhead)

prompt: Which probe can gate liveness and readiness until initial startup succeeds?
scenario: A container legitimately needs 90 seconds to initialize, but ordinary liveness checks keep restarting it before initialization finishes.

options.text: A new hostname without changing probe behavior
An even shorter liveness failure threshold

explanation: A startup probe delays liveness and readiness checks until it succeeds. Its failure threshold and period must allow the expected initialization time. Source: [Kubernetes probes](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/workloads/pods/probes/)

prompt: Which recovery objective is missed in the worst case?
scenario: Backups are four hours apart, with no later recoverable log. The required RPO is one hour and RTO is 30 minutes. Restoration takes ten minutes.

options.text: RTO and RPO mean the same thing
Neither objective can ever be met by any system

explanation: RPO constrains tolerable data loss measured from the recovery point. Fast restoration can satisfy RTO while an old backup still misses the RPO. Source: [AWS recovery objectives](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/wellarchitected/latest/reliability-pillar/rel_planning_for_recovery_objective_defined_recovery.html)

prompt: Order a basic canary evaluation before a broad rollout.

options.text: Choose representative traffic, comparison metrics and stop criteria
Send a small controlled share to the new version
Compare canary and control over an adequate sample and window
Expand if criteria pass, or stop and investigate if they fail

explanation: A useful canary compares a representative sample against the control and service objectives. A few successful requests alone are not sufficient evidence for expansion. Source: [Google SRE canaries](https://sre.google/workbook/canarying-releases/)
